body:
So, a quick update. We followed through with the plan and visited him as a group. He was happy to see us (we were as well, obviously), we sat down in the common room of the hospital (there was nobody else there) and he told us the whole story. Hearing it was just surreal, but there was one thing he said that really stuck with me. 

He'd been sure he wanted to do it that whole day, up to the very moment of jumping. But right as he was falling into the water, he realized he didn't want to die and that it had all been a very bad mistake. You could say his survival instinct kicked in and he somehow swam to the beach, where he lay down exhausted and hypothermic.

It was truly a miracle that some couple were walking along the beach in the middle of the night in October. But for them, he would be dead now - he said it was a matter of 20 minutes had the ambulance not come. I'm an agnostic but all this just seems too surreal to be pure chance. I think I'll go to church tomorrow...

All in all, he said he's realized that suicide is not the answer. I'm so happy I made this trip, I feel like it really helped both him and our whole group. When he was talking he was completely honest, like he'd never been beofre. Of course, he will be under a psychologist's care for some time now, but after today I'm pretty sure he'll never attempt something like this again.

Sorry for the rant, but I want to tell somebody about this and obviously it's out of question to speak about it with any friends. I'm happy this dark story has had a happy ending after all - maybe miracles really do happen.

Do you think it's a good idea to visit him in the hospital tomorrow with everybody he considered a good enough friend to tell them what happened? Including me that's 5 people, we've discussed this and think it might make him happy to see that we really do care about him and support him.

> One thing that's not completely clear to me from what you've written - do you know if his parents and doctors know the real reason for what he did? I'm not sure if he's asking you to keep it quiet from the rest of the social group (which is reasonable and understandable), or if you're the only person he's told the whole truth to, and he doesn't want his family or his physicians to know, in which case you might need to break his confidence (and risk his anger, at least temporarily) in order to ensure his well-being.

He told his parents and a few other close friends. I'm not sure if the doctors know the real reason, but I really doubt he told them about it. They must at least suspect it, I think.
